\documentclass[11pt]{article}
\usepackage[margin=1in]{geometry}
\usepackage{amsmath}
\usepackage{amssymb}
\usepackage{amsthm}

\newtheorem{theorem}{Theorem}
\newtheorem{lemma}[theorem]{Lemma}
\newtheorem{definition}[theorem]{Definition}

\title{Tight Convergence Rates for Bilevel\\Stochastic Optimization}
\author{C.~Vasquez and D.~Whitfield}
\date{March 2026}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
We study bilevel stochastic optimization when the lower-level problem
can only be solved approximately. We give a double-loop algorithm that
finds an $\epsilon$-stationary point with $O(\epsilon^{-2})$ stochastic
gradient evaluations, and we prove a matching lower bound showing that
the dependence on $\epsilon$ cannot be improved. The analysis
introduces a surrogate descent function that decouples the bias of the
lower-level estimate from the variance of the hypergradient.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
Bilevel formulations are a workhorse model for meta-learning,
hyperparameter search, and neural architecture design. In their
classical form, the lower-level solution is assumed to be computed
exactly before each upper-level update. In most applications, however,
the lower-level problem is itself stochastic and high-dimensional: a
model must be (approximately) retrained before a hyperparameter can be
evaluated. The algorithm must then trade inner-loop accuracy against
outer-loop progress, which couples optimization error with statistical
error.

This paper isolates that trade-off in the simplest nontrivial setting.
The lower-level objective is smooth and strongly convex, the
upper-level objective is smooth but possibly nonconvex, and access to
both objectives is through a stochastic gradient oracle with bounded
variance. The goal is to find an $\epsilon$-stationary point of the
upper-level value function with as few oracle calls as possible.

Our main result is a double-loop algorithm that needs
$O(\epsilon^{-2})$ oracle calls, where the inner loop runs
$\Theta(\log(1/\epsilon))$ steps per outer iteration. We complement
the upper bound with a lower bound of the same order, which shows that
no algorithm interacting with the same oracle can do better by more
than logarithmic factors.

\section{Preliminaries}
Let $f(x, y)$ denote the upper-level objective and $g(x, y)$ the
lower-level objective, with $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ the upper-level
variable and $y \in \mathbb{R}^p$ the lower-level variable. Write
$y^*(x) = \arg\min_y g(x, y)$ and $F(x) = f(x, y^*(x))$. The oracle
returns, for any query point $(x, y)$, unbiased estimates of
$\nabla_x f$, $\nabla_y f$, and $\nabla_y g$ with variance at most
$\sigma^2$.

\begin{definition}[$\epsilon$-stationarity]
A point $x$ is $\epsilon$-stationary for the bilevel problem if
$\| \nabla F(x) \| \le \epsilon$, where $F$ is the upper-level value
function defined above.
\end{definition}

We assume that $g$ is $\mu$-strongly convex in $y$ and that all
gradients are $L$-Lipschitz in both variables. The approximate
hypergradient obtained by backpropagating through $K$ inner steps is
denoted $\widetilde{\nabla} F(x)$; its bias decays exponentially in
$K$ under the assumptions above.

\section{The Double-Loop Algorithm}
The algorithm alternates between $K$ steps of stochastic gradient
descent on the lower-level problem and one hypergradient step on the
upper-level variable. The inner loop starts from the previous
lower-level estimate, which warm-starts the optimization once the
outer iterates stabilize.

\begin{theorem}[Upper bound]\label{thm:upper}
With $K = \Theta(\log(1/\epsilon))$ inner steps and step size
$\eta = \Theta(1/L)$, the double-loop algorithm returns an
$\epsilon$-stationary point within $O(\epsilon^{-2})$ oracle calls.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
We decompose the optimality gap into the sum, over outer iterations,
of the expected descent contributed by each hypergradient step minus
the bias injected by the inner loop. By the warm-start construction,
the lower-level error contracts by a constant factor per outer
iteration, so the cumulative bias is dominated by its first term.
Summing the descent lemma over $T = O(\epsilon^{-2})$ outer iterations
and choosing the step size to balance the descent and bias terms gives
$\min_t \| \nabla F(x_t) \|^2 \le 4 (F(x_0) - F^*) / (\eta T)$, which
yields the stated oracle complexity once the inner-loop length is
substituted.
\end{proof}

The analysis relies on a descent lemma that separates the curvature of
$F$ from the bias of the hypergradient estimate.

\begin{lemma}[Descent]\label{lem:descent}
Let $x_{t+1} = x_t - \eta \widetilde{\nabla} F(x_t)$ and let
$\delta_t = \| \widetilde{\nabla} F(x_t) - \nabla F(x_t) \|^2$. Then
\[
F(x_{t+1}) \le F(x_t) - \frac{\eta}{2} \| \nabla F(x_t) \|^2 + \eta \delta_t,
\]
provided $\eta \le 1/L$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
By the $L$-smoothness of $F$, the quadratic upper bound gives
$F(x_{t+1}) \le F(x_t) + \langle \nabla F(x_t), x_{t+1} - x_t \rangle
+ (L/2) \| x_{t+1} - x_t \|^2$. Substituting the update and expanding
the inner product as the sum of a descent term and a bias term,
\[
\langle \nabla F(x_t), -\widetilde{\nabla} F(x_t) \rangle
= -\| \nabla F(x_t) \|^2 + \langle \nabla F(x_t), \nabla F(x_t) - \widetilde{\nabla} F(x_t) \rangle,
\]
and applying Young's inequality to the cross term with coefficient
$1/2$ yields the claim whenever $\eta \le 1/L$.
\end{proof}

\section{Lower Bound}
The upper bound is matched by a lower bound that holds even when the
lower-level problem is exactly quadratic.

\begin{theorem}[Lower bound]\label{thm:lower}
For every algorithm interacting with the objectives through the
stochastic gradient oracle, there exists an instance on which at least
$\Omega(\epsilon^{-2})$ oracle calls are required to return an
$\epsilon$-stationary point.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Consider a family of instances in which the lower-level problem is a
fixed strongly convex quadratic and the upper-level objective is a
stochastic quadratic whose mean gradient encodes one of $m$ possible
linear functions. In instance $I_j$, the gradient noise is Gaussian
with variance $\sigma^2$ except along coordinate $j$, where the mean
gradient is larger by $\epsilon$ with $\epsilon = \sigma / \sqrt{T}$.
Each oracle call reveals one noisy gradient. A standard pinning
argument shows that any algorithm that identifies the informative
coordinate with probability above $2/3$ must query the remaining
coordinates $\Omega(\sigma^2 / \epsilon^2)$ times in expectation.
Summing the resulting stationarity gap over the $m$ coordinates and
choosing $\epsilon$ to balance the identification and optimization
terms gives the stated lower bound, and an averaging argument over $j$
yields the single hard instance.
\end{proof}

\section{Discussion}
The logarithmic inner-loop length in the upper bound is unavoidable
when the lower-level estimate can only be refined by stochastic
gradients, because the first inner step of each outer iteration runs
without any curvature information. The remaining gap between the upper
and lower bounds is a logarithmic factor in $1/\epsilon$, which we
conjecture can be removed by a more careful stability argument.

Several extensions are natural. When the lower-level objective admits
a closed-form solution, the inner loop can be replaced by direct
evaluation and the logarithmic factor disappears. When gradient noise
is correlated across iterations, our analysis extends with only
notational changes. We leave the constrained setting, which requires
combining bilevel optimization with projection oracles, to future
work.

\section{Conclusion}
We have given matching upper and lower bounds for bilevel stochastic
optimization, establishing that the price of an inexact lower level
scales as $\epsilon^{-2}$ up to logarithmic factors. The double-loop
algorithm is simple to implement given any stochastic inner solver,
and the surrogate-descent technique decouples the optimization and
statistical difficulties in a way that we expect to transfer to other
nested problems with inexact oracles.
\end{document}
